title: Valuation Framework
purpose: Choose valuation methods that fit the business, understand their limits, and compare conclusions without false precision.

overview.designedToAnswer: Choose valuation methods that fit the business, understand their limits, and compare conclusions without false precision.
overview.whenToUse: When applying the author's valuation approach as part of a broader research process.
overview.whenNotToUse: As a substitute for evidence, a current company assessment, or a mechanically generated investment recommendation.

content.text: "What is this company worth?" It looks like a mathematical problem. It isn't. If valuation were simply plugging numbers into a spreadsheet, every analyst would reach the same answer. They don't. Ask ten experienced investors to value the same company and you'll probably receive ten slightly different estimates. Ask them during a market crash and you'll receive ten very different estimates. That isn't because valuation models are useless.

It's because businesses are living, evolving systems. They hire people. Launch products. Lose customers. Enter new markets. Face regulations. Respond to competitors. No spreadsheet can perfectly capture all of that. Throughout finance literature, valuation has always been presented as both an art and a science. The science lies in financial modelling. The art lies in selecting assumptions that reasonably reflect reality. Personally, I think the biggest mistake investors make isn't choosing the wrong valuation model.

It's believing there is a single correct model. Every valuation method answers a different question. A Discounted Cash Flow model asks, "What are this company's future cash flows worth today?" A Price-to-Earnings ratio asks, "How much are investors willing to pay for current earnings?" Enterprise Value multiples ask, "What is the market paying for the operating business regardless of capital structure?" Each provides a different piece of the puzzle.
The challenge is learning when each piece becomes useful.

Finding a great business is only half the investment decision. Buying that business at the wrong price can still produce disappointing returns. History offers countless examples. During the dot-com bubble, many outstanding technology companies traded at extraordinary valuations. Several eventually became exceptional businesses. Some investors still lost money because they paid far too much. The business succeeded. The investment didn't. That distinction is important. Price matters.
Quality matters. Ignoring either usually creates problems.

The Discounted Cash Flow model is frequently described as the gold standard of valuation. The idea is beautifully logical. A business is worth the cash it will generate in the future, adjusted for the time value of money. Future cash flows are estimated. Each year's cash flow is discounted back to today's value using a required rate of return. Those discounted cash flows are then added together.

Finally, a terminal value estimates the company's value beyond the explicit forecast period. Conceptually, the model makes perfect sense. In practice, however, DCF models are extremely sensitive to assumptions. Small adjustments to revenue growth, operating margins or discount rates can change valuations dramatically. Personally, I think DCF works best when analysing mature businesses with relatively predictable cash flows.
Strengths

items: Encourages detailed understanding of the business

content.text: Limitations

items: Terminal value often dominates total valuation
Less reliable for young or rapidly changing businesses

content.text: Relative valuation takes a very different approach. Instead of asking, "What is this company worth?" it asks, "What are similar companies worth?" The logic is straightforward. If two businesses possess comparable growth rates, profitability and competitive positions, they should trade at broadly similar valuation multiples. This method dominates practical investing because it is fast, intuitive and widely understood. However, it also introduces an important risk.

Markets occasionally misprice entire industries. Comparing one expensive company with another expensive company may simply confirm that both are expensive. Relative valuation therefore measures relative attractiveness, not necessarily intrinsic value. Personally, I think it works best as a reality check rather than a final decision-maker.

Enterprise Value divided by EBITDA has become one of the most widely used valuation multiples in professional finance. Unlike equity-based ratios, EV/EBITDA considers the value of the entire business, including debt. This makes comparisons between companies with different financing structures considerably easier. Because EBITDA excludes interest, taxes and certain accounting expenses, it provides a cleaner view of operating performance. Private equity firms frequently rely on this multiple because it focuses primarily on operating profitability.

That said, EBITDA has limitations. Depreciation and capital expenditure may be accounting expenses, but real businesses eventually need to replace equipment, factories and infrastructure. Ignoring those costs entirely can produce overly optimistic conclusions.
Strengths

items: Excellent for comparing companies across industries
Widely used in mergers and acquisitions

content.text: Limitations

items: EBITDA is not free cash flow

content.text: The Price-to-Earnings ratio is probably the world's most recognised valuation metric. Its popularity comes from simplicity. It measures how much investors are willing to pay for one dollar of earnings. High P/E ratios usually suggest high growth expectations. Low P/E ratios may indicate pessimism—or opportunity. The challenge lies in determining which interpretation is correct. A low P/E can represent undervaluation. It can also represent a declining business.
Similarly, high P/E ratios occasionally reflect irrational optimism. Sometimes they simply reflect extraordinary business quality.
Strengths
Limitations

items: Does not directly measure cash generation

content.text: Some businesses generate little or no profit despite producing substantial revenue. Traditional earnings multiples become difficult to apply. Price-to-Sales solves this problem by focusing on revenue instead. The ratio became particularly popular during the growth-stock era when many technology companies prioritised expansion over profitability. Personally, I think Price-to-Sales should always be interpreted alongside operating margins. Revenue without profitability is interesting. Revenue with improving profitability is considerably more interesting.
Strengths
Limitations

items: High sales do not guarantee strong businesses
Can overvalue companies with weak margins

content.text: The PEG Ratio attempts to solve one of the biggest criticisms of the P/E ratio. Growth matters. Two companies trading at thirty times earnings are not necessarily equally expensive if one grows earnings at 5% annually while the other grows at 30%. The PEG ratio adjusts the P/E multiple by expected earnings growth. A lower PEG often suggests better value relative to growth expectations. Like every valuation metric, however, it depends heavily on forecasting future growth accurately.
Forecasting is difficult enough. Forecasting five years into the future occasionally feels like predicting next year's weather using today's clouds. Possible. Not guaranteed.
Strengths
Limitations
One of the biggest mistakes investors make is using the same valuation tool for every business. Different companies deserve different approaches.

content.text: Personally, I don't think investors should ask, "Which valuation method is best?" A better question is, "Which method best matches the economics of this business?"
DCF — The Microscope
Looks deep into intrinsic value. Excellent when future cash flows are relatively predictable. Slow. Detailed. Powerful.
Relative Valuation — The Mirror
Shows how the market currently values similar businesses. Quick. Practical. Useful for benchmarking.
EV/EBITDA — The X-Ray
Looks through financing decisions to examine operating performance. Excellent for acquisitions and mature operating businesses.
P/E — The Speedometer
Shows how expensive current earnings appear. Simple. Fast. Easy to interpret. But it doesn't explain why the speed changed.
P/S — The Telescope
Useful for spotting potential in businesses that haven't yet reached profitability. Great for seeing far ahead. Less useful for measuring today's earnings power.
PEG — The Compass

Balances valuation with growth expectations. Helpful when growth is the central investment story. No single tool replaces the others. The best mechanics don't carry one wrench. The best investors shouldn't rely on one multiple.
Layer One — Understand the Business

Before opening Excel, answer three questions: Does the company have a durable moat? Is management competent? Can earnings compound over time? If the answer is "no," valuation becomes much less interesting.
Layer Two — Choose the Right Tool
Not every company deserves a DCF. Not every company deserves a P/E comparison. Select the method that fits the business model rather than forcing the business into the model.
Layer Three — Compare Results

Run more than one valuation method. If DCF, EV/EBITDA and peer comparisons all point toward similar conclusions, confidence naturally increases. If one method says the company is worth twice as much as every other method suggests... don't celebrate. Investigate. Sometimes you've found a market opportunity. More often, you've found an assumption that deserves another look.

content.text: Valuation is often presented as the final stage of investment analysis. Personally, I think it belongs much closer to the end than the beginning. A perfectly valued business with weak fundamentals remains a weak investment. An outstanding business deserves attention before its price ever enters the discussion. The methods explored in this chapter—DCF, relative valuation, EV/EBITDA, P/E, P/S and PEG—are not competing philosophies. They are complementary perspectives.

Each reveals something useful. Each hides something else. The responsibility of the investor is not to find the "perfect" valuation model. It is to understand what every model can—and cannot—tell you. If I had to summarise this framework in one sentence, it would be this: Valuation is less about finding a single precise answer and more about narrowing a range of reasonable answers until price and business quality begin telling the same story.
After all, spreadsheets are excellent at calculating numbers. They are considerably less talented at calculating common sense. Good investors still have to supply that part themselves.

content.text: One red flag isn't fatal. Five usually tell a story.

Before buying any company, I ask myself five final questions: If the stock market closed for five years, would I still want to own this business? Can I explain its business model without using buzzwords? Does it earn high returns because it's genuinely better, or because conditions are temporarily favorable? Would I be happy if the stock fell 30% tomorrow, knowing I'd own more of the same business?
Am I buying the company—or simply buying a popular story? If I hesitate on more than one answer, I usually keep researching.

After studying dozens of companies, I've realized something slightly disappointing. There isn't a magical ratio. There isn't a secret spreadsheet. There isn't a single number that identifies the next great investment. Great investing is usually just asking good questions consistently. That's what this scorecard is designed to do. It's not meant to replace judgment—it exists to sharpen it. A company can still earn a mediocre score and outperform because of an unexpected breakthrough. Likewise, a 95/100 company can become a poor investment if purchased at a ridiculous price.

The score isn't the destination. The conversation it forces you to have with the business is. Or, put another way: A checklist won't guarantee you find the next Visa. But it might stop you from accidentally buying the next company that promises to "revolutionize everything" and ends up revolutionizing only your portfolio's ability to lose money.

title: Market Cycles Framework
purpose: Understand how economic conditions and investor psychology affect business analysis without pretending to predict turning points.

overview.designedToAnswer: Understand how economic conditions and investor psychology affect business analysis without pretending to predict turning points.
overview.whenToUse: When applying the author's market cycles approach as part of a broader research process.
overview.whenNotToUse: As a substitute for evidence, a current company assessment, or a mechanically generated investment recommendation.

content.text: Many investors spend enormous amounts of time trying to predict which stock will outperform next year. Far fewer spend equal time understanding the environment in which those companies operate. That is a mistake. Even exceptional businesses rarely escape the influence of broader economic conditions. Interest rates affect borrowing costs. Inflation changes consumer spending. Recessions reduce business investment. Recoveries restore confidence. The same company can produce excellent financial results while experiencing dramatically different stock market performance depending on where the economy sits within the broader cycle.

Personally, I think understanding market cycles does not make someone a better market timer. It makes them a better decision-maker. There is an important difference. The objective is not predicting the exact month a recession begins. The objective is recognising how different environments influence businesses differently.

Bull markets are periods of sustained optimism. Economic activity expands. Corporate earnings generally improve. Employment rises. Consumer confidence strengthens. Investors become increasingly willing to take risk. Stock prices typically rise over extended periods. Interestingly, bull markets rarely begin with widespread optimism. They often begin quietly. The economy starts improving. Corporate profits stabilise. Fear gradually fades. Only later, after prices have already risen significantly, does widespread enthusiasm appear.

That sequence matters. Optimism usually follows rising prices. It rarely causes the first stage of recovery. As confidence grows, capital flows into equities. Companies raise money more easily. Businesses invest. Consumers spend. Positive feedback begins reinforcing itself. Bull markets therefore become partially economic events and partially psychological events. The longer they continue, the more investors begin believing they will never end. History politely disagrees.
Characteristics of Bull Markets
Personally, I think the greatest danger during bull markets isn't excessive optimism. It's forgetting that optimism itself eventually becomes part of the risk.

Bear markets represent the opposite phase. Confidence weakens. Growth slows. Corporate earnings disappoint. Investors become increasingly cautious. Prices decline. Risk suddenly feels much less fashionable. Interestingly, markets often fall long before the economy reaches its weakest point. Investors continuously attempt to price the future rather than the present. This explains why markets occasionally begin recovering while economic headlines remain overwhelmingly negative. To someone unfamiliar with market cycles, this behaviour seems irrational.

In reality, markets simply spend most of their time looking ahead. Bear markets also expose business quality remarkably well. Weak companies frequently struggle to survive. Strong companies often emerge even stronger. Personally, I think bear markets perform the same function for businesses that stress tests perform for bridges. Nobody enjoys them. Everyone benefits from knowing what survives them.
Characteristics of Bear Markets
One lesson appears repeatedly throughout history. Bear markets eventually end. Unfortunately, nobody sends investors a calendar invitation beforehand.

A recession represents a slowdown in overall economic activity. Businesses reduce investment. Consumers spend more cautiously. Industrial production weakens. Employment often declines. Although recessions frequently coincide with bear markets, the two concepts are not identical. Markets sometimes decline without a recession. Recessions occasionally occur after markets have already begun recovering. That distinction is important. Economic data generally describes what has happened. Markets attempt to price what may happen next.

Personally, I think investors often underestimate how adaptable strong businesses become during recessions. Companies with healthy balance sheets frequently use downturns to invest, acquire competitors and strengthen market positions. Weak economies sometimes create surprisingly attractive long-term opportunities.
Recoveries

Recoveries are probably the most misunderstood phase of every market cycle. Why? Because they rarely feel like recoveries. News headlines remain negative. Economic data still appears disappointing. Consumer confidence remains fragile. Yet markets often begin rising anyway. Recovery begins when conditions stop getting worse rather than suddenly becoming excellent. That difference is subtle. It is also incredibly important. Many investors wait for perfect certainty before investing.

Markets rarely provide it. By the time optimism becomes obvious, much of the recovery has already occurred. Personally, I think patience matters most during recoveries. Not because investing becomes easy. Because uncertainty remains high even while opportunities quietly improve.

Interest rates influence almost every financial asset. When borrowing becomes cheaper, businesses invest more readily. Consumers purchase homes, vehicles and other large purchases more comfortably. Economic activity generally accelerates. When central banks increase interest rates, borrowing becomes more expensive. Consumer demand often slows. Business investment moderates. Inflation gradually cools. Financial markets respond quickly because future corporate earnings become discounted at higher rates. Growth companies typically experience larger valuation changes because more of their expected value lies further into the future.

Personally, I don't think interest rates determine which companies succeed. They influence how investors value those companies. That distinction explains why outstanding businesses sometimes experience significant price declines despite continuing operational success.

Inflation quietly influences almost every business decision. Higher input costs. Changing wages. Consumer purchasing power. Corporate pricing decisions. Interest-rate policy. Persistent inflation creates uncertainty because businesses struggle to forecast future costs accurately. Some companies possess strong pricing power. Others do not. This is where competitive advantages become particularly valuable. Businesses with durable brands or essential products often pass higher costs to customers more successfully than commodity businesses.
Interestingly, inflation often separates genuine pricing power from temporary popularity. Anyone can raise prices. Not everyone can persuade customers to keep buying afterwards.

If economics explains half of market cycles, psychology explains the other half. Human emotions change surprisingly little across generations. Optimism. Fear. Greed. Regret. Overconfidence. Panic. Every market cycle contains each of them. Technology changes. The emotions behind investing remain remarkably familiar. Investors buy aggressively because prices have already risen. They sell aggressively because prices have already fallen. Ironically, both decisions frequently occur at precisely the wrong time.
One observation became increasingly clear while researching behavioural finance. Markets rarely create emotional mistakes. They expose emotional mistakes that already existed.
Spring — Recovery
Confidence slowly returns. Businesses stabilise. Valuations remain reasonable. Opportunities quietly emerge. Most investors remain cautious.
️ Summer — Expansion
Growth accelerates. Corporate earnings improve. Employment strengthens. Optimism spreads. Businesses invest confidently.
Autumn — Euphoria
Valuations become increasingly stretched. Speculation rises. Investors begin believing "this time is different." History quietly starts taking notes.
️ Winter — Contraction

Economic activity slows. Fear dominates. Weak businesses struggle. Strong businesses prepare for the next cycle. Winter feels permanent. It never is. Personally, I find this framework more useful than trying to predict precise market turning points. Recognising the season often matters more than predicting tomorrow's weather.

Market cycles are often described as forces investors should fear. Personally, I think they should be viewed differently. They are simply part of investing. Just as businesses experience periods of rapid growth and slower expansion, economies experience cycles of optimism and contraction. Markets reflect those changes. The objective is not to predict every cycle perfectly. History suggests very few people consistently achieve that. The objective is to understand how different environments influence business quality, valuation and investor behaviour.

Bull markets reward optimism. Bear markets reward patience. Recoveries reward conviction. Recessions reward discipline. And throughout every phase, exceptional businesses continue doing what they have always done—adapting. If I had to summarise this entire framework in one sentence, it would be this: Market cycles change the prices investors pay for businesses far more frequently than they change the underlying quality of those businesses. That is why the best investors spend less time trying to predict the next market cycle and more time ensuring the businesses they own are capable of surviving every one of them.
Because sooner or later, another cycle always arrives.

title: Economic Moat Measurement Framework
purpose: Organize evidence about moat strength through seven weighted dimensions while keeping judgment and valuation separate.

overview.designedToAnswer: Organize evidence about moat strength through seven weighted dimensions while keeping judgment and valuation separate.
overview.whenToUse: When applying the author's economic moat measurement approach as part of a broader research process.
overview.whenNotToUse: As a substitute for evidence, a current company assessment, or a mechanically generated investment recommendation.

content.text: Rather than asking whether a company has a moat, this chapter builds a practical scoring system that estimates how wide, durable and defensible that moat actually is. Naturally, no framework can remove judgement entirely. Business quality is not something that can be measured with a ruler. However, structured thinking usually produces better decisions than relying purely on intuition. Personally, I don't think the goal is mathematical precision.

The goal is making comparisons more consistent. If two businesses receive similar scores, investors should understand why. If they receive dramatically different scores, that difference should be supported by evidence rather than instinct.
Brand Strength

A powerful brand allows companies to charge premium prices, attract loyal customers and withstand competitive pressure. Strong brands reduce customer uncertainty. People often purchase brands they already trust because uncertainty carries its own cost. Luxury companies demonstrate this clearly.
Indicators
Network Effects
Network effects occur when a product becomes more valuable as additional users join. Mastercard provides an excellent example. More cardholders attract more merchants.
Indicators
Switching Costs

Some businesses make leaving surprisingly expensive. Not necessarily financially. Operationally. Technically. Psychologically. Enterprise software illustrates this well. Changing systems often requires employee retraining, data migration and operational disruption. Many businesses continue using existing software simply because switching would be painful. Switching costs therefore protect existing revenue even without dramatic innovation.
Indicators
Cost Advantage
Companies with structural cost advantages can produce goods or services more efficiently than competitors. Lower costs allow either:
Lower selling prices. Sometimes both.
Indicators
Intangible Assets
Some competitive advantages exist almost entirely on paper. Patents. Licenses. Trademarks. Copyrights.
Indicators
Scale Advantage

Large businesses often become more efficient simply because of their size. Scale improves purchasing power. Marketing efficiency. Distribution. Research spending. Negotiating leverage. Fixed costs become spread across larger operations. This advantage explains why dominant companies frequently continue strengthening their market positions. Scale alone does not guarantee success. Combined with good management, however, it becomes remarkably powerful.
Indicators
Regulatory Advantages
Certain businesses benefit from regulations that unintentionally discourage competition.
Indicators

To transform qualitative analysis into something investors can compare more consistently, I developed the Moat Score Framework. Each source of competitive advantage receives a weighted score based on its long-term importance.

The weighting reflects a simple observation. Some competitive advantages compound more effectively than others. A great brand or powerful network often strengthens itself over time. Cost advantages and patents matter greatly, but they may be easier to challenge than a deeply embedded ecosystem.

content.text: One important point deserves emphasis. A high Moat Score does not automatically make a stock a good investment. A wonderful business purchased at an unreasonable price can still produce poor returns. Likewise, a business with a modest moat may become attractive if the market has become excessively pessimistic. The Moat Score should therefore be viewed as one pillar of investment analysis, alongside valuation, financial statement quality, management, industry structure and macroeconomic conditions.

Economic moats are often discussed as though they are mysterious qualities that investors either recognise or miss. I don't think they're mysterious. They're observable. They can be questioned, challenged and compared. This framework does not claim to measure competitive advantage with scientific precision. Businesses are too complex for that. What it does provide is a disciplined way of organising evidence before reaching a conclusion. Instead of saying, "This feels like a great company," investors can explain why it deserves that reputation.

If I had to summarise this framework in one sentence, it would be this: A company's moat is strongest not when it excels in one category, but when several independent advantages reinforce one another until competing becomes economically unattractive. In investing, the best businesses don't win because they're impossible to compete with. They win because, after looking at everything required to catch them, most competitors decide it simply isn't worth trying.
